whyItExists.problem: Promise chains with .then().then().catch() can still become hard to follow, especially with conditional logic or loops. The indentation and callback structure feels foreign to synchronous code.
whyItExists.solution: async/await is syntax sugar over Promises. async makes a function return a Promise. await pauses execution inside an async function until a Promise resolves — making async code look and behave like synchronous code.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any async code that uses Promises — HTTP requests, file I/O, database queries, timeouts. Prefer async/await over raw .then() chains for readability.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Top-level await only works in ES modules or with a wrapper. Avoid async in forEach — use for...of instead. Don't use await in a tight loop for parallel operations — use Promise.all.

explainModes.beginner: async makes a function 'pauseable'. Inside it, await makes JavaScript wait for a slow operation (like a network request) before moving on. Write it like normal code — no .then() chains.
explainModes.simple: async function fetchData() { const res = await fetch('/api'); const data = await res.json(); return data; } — each await line waits for the promise to resolve before the next line runs.
explainModes.standard: An async function always returns a Promise, even if you return a plain value. await can only be used inside an async function (or top-level in an ES module). Use try/catch to handle errors — it catches rejected Promises just like thrown errors.
explainModes.technical: async/await is transpiled to Promise chains by Babel/TypeScript. The JavaScript engine suspends the async function at each await, freeing the event loop to process other work. Calling an async function returns a Promise immediately — the caller can await it or use .then(). Parallel execution: const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()]) runs both requests simultaneously.
explainModes.deepDive: Under the hood, async functions are generators that automatically yield at each await. Top-level await in ES modules allows await at module scope. AbortController and AbortSignal let you cancel fetch requests mid-await. The for await...of construct iterates asynchronous iterables (like readable streams from the Fetch API) one chunk at a time.

content.text: Do NOT use async inside forEach — it doesn't await the callbacks. Use for...of instead: for (const item of items) { await process(item); }

questions.question: What does an async function always return?
questions.explanation: An async function always returns a Promise. If you return a plain value, it is wrapped in Promise.resolve(value). This means callers can use .then() or await on it.

questions.question: How do you run two async operations in parallel with async/await?
questions.explanation: await op1(); await op2(); runs them sequentially. To run in parallel, start both promises first and await them together with Promise.all: const [r1, r2] = await Promise.all([op1(), op2()]).

faq.q: Can I use await outside an async function?
faq.a: In ES modules (type='module'), top-level await is supported. In classic scripts, you need to wrap code in an async IIFE: (async () => { const data = await fetch(...); })().

faq.q: Does await block the entire browser?
faq.a: No. await only suspends the current async function — other code, event listeners, and rendering continue normally. JavaScript is still single-threaded, but await yields control back to the event loop.

usedIn: every React hook that fetches data
examples: React: useEffect(() => { (async () => { const data = await fetchPosts(); setPosts(data); })(); }, [])
Express: app.get('/users', async (req, res) => { const users = await db.find(); res.json(users); })
Next.js: export async function getServerSideProps() { const data = await fetch(...); return { props: data }; }
